hints: Look closely at the structure of one adult haemoglobin molecule, not just the total number. How many polypeptide chains make it up, and how many of those are specifically alpha chains?
Once you know the number of alpha chains per haemoglobin, multiply 260 million by that number, then rewrite your answer in standard form as $a \times 10^n$ to match the options.
walkthrough:
**Recall what one haemoglobin is made of**

Think of one haemoglobin molecule like a little team of four. In a healthy adult it is $2$ alpha-globin chains plus $2$ beta-globin chains.

So per haemoglobin:
$$ \text{alpha chains} = 2 $$

**Multiply up for the whole red blood cell**

One cell has 260 million haemoglobins, and each one brings 2 alphas with it. So we just multiply.
$$ 260,000,000 \times 2 = 520,000,000 $$

**Convert to standard form and choose**

520 million is 520 x one million. In standard form that is:
$$ 5.2 \times 10^8 $$
That matches option C exactly. Well done, it is just structure recall plus one simple multiplication.

options.A: This is half of 260 million. It comes from dividing by 2 instead of multiplying by 2 alpha chains per haemoglobin.
options.B: This is just 260 million written as $2.6 \times 10^8$. It assumes only 1 alpha chain per haemoglobin, forgetting the molecule has 2 alphas.
options.C: Correct. Each haemoglobin has 2 alpha chains, so $260 \text{ million} \times 2 = 520 \text{ million} = 5.2 \times 10^8$.
options.D: This is $260 \text{ million} \times 4$. It counts all 4 globin chains (2 alpha + 2 beta) instead of just the alpha chains.
